summary:
Malaysia criminalises both same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity at two levels, and Kedah stands under that national framework. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, carrying a maximum of 20 years plus whipping; these provisions are not limited to Malaysians and apply to visitors. Every one of the 13 states and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya additionally maintains a Sharia enactment criminalising cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Those state offences reach Muslims only.

Kedah's own instrument is the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kedah Darul Aman) Enactment 2014 (En.18/2014). Sections 23 and 24 criminalise liwat (sodomy) and musahaqah (lesbian sex), punishable by a fine of up to RM5,000, up to three years' imprisonment or up to six strokes of whipping, or any combination of those penalties. Section 26 criminalises a male posing as a woman in public, carrying a fine of up to RM1,000 or up to one year's imprisonment. Female cross-dressing is not an offence under the enactment.

Enforcement in Kedah has reached trans women and the people around them. Malay Mail reported on 30 October 2020 that a private birthday party had been raided, that 30 trans women were singled out and arrested, and that a coalition of Malaysian human-rights groups expressed concern over a subsequent probe of the Kedah event organiser for "encouraging vice". The case shows organisers and allies of transgender persons being proceeded against alongside trans people themselves.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor, the Kedah Sharia offences do not apply, but the federal Penal Code does. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops.
tangentialFactors:
Litigation has narrowed the state Sharia layer without loosening the federal one. The High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional, and the Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, leaving Penal Code offences fully intact. A constitutional challenge was pending as of late 2014 following the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014. No challenge to Kedah's section 26 is documented in the sources.

Kedah's section 26 is narrower than the national pattern: since the 1980s all 13 states have passed cross-dressing enactments, and three of them also bar women from posing as men. Kedah's enactment does not.

Enforcement against gender nonconformity elsewhere in Malaysia is active and public. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) had his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked. In the Nur Sajat case, 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her for "insulting Islam" before she fled to Thailand and received UNHCR protection.

Queue-and-venue raids carry acute exposure risk. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, arresting 208 men under section 377B in the largest operation of its kind since 2022. Media were pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were leaked; 17 civil servants identified among them were suspended. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground, yet release was delayed, with more than 130 people held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid; on 2 December the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang.

Trans people in Malaysia face lethal violence and official indifference to it. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months; documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself".
localsOnly:
Muslims in Kedah are subject to sections 23, 24 and 26 of the state enactment. Section 52 goes further for women: a woman convicted of musahaqah may additionally be committed to an approved home for up to six months.

The Sharia laws contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing, and enforcement is carried out by state Islamic religious departments.

The wider climate is one of state-backed restriction. Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects, government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and LGBT events and media content are censored. There is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2020 probe of the Kedah event organiser concluded, and with what outcome, is not sourced here.

Whether Kedah's section 26 has been subject to constitutional or federalism litigation is unresolved in the sources; only the Selangor and Kelantan challenges are documented.

The sources state that three states also bar women from posing as men but do not identify which three. Kedah's own enactment does not.

No Kedah-specific figures on caning sentences, remand practice or raid frequency appear in the inventory.

Whether the Home Minister's December 2025 suggestion of revisiting section 377 produced legislative change is unresolved.
